summary: This document describes requirements for a BGP security protocol design. The design should give cryptographic assurance that an origin AS has the right to announce a prefix, and assurance of the AS path in the announcement.

plainLanguage.summary: BGP is how networks tell each other which roads lead where, but anyone can lie. This RFC lists what a secure version needs so you can check who may announce a route and the path it took.

questions: how to secure bgp as path
how does bgpsec prevent route hijacking
subtitle: What a secure BGP protocol must do to prevent route hijacking

tldr.problem: BGP allows any AS to announce any route, and the AS path in a route announcement can be modified in transit. This opens the door to route hijacking attacks.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies requirements for a security protocol called BGPsec that must cryptographically verify that the originating AS has the right to announce a prefix, and that the AS path has not been modified.
tldr.outcome: It establishes a comprehensive set of 30 security requirements that any BGP security design must satisfy. Later RFCs implement these requirements.

today: RFC 7353 is still the reference for BGP security protocol requirements. RFC 8205 implements these requirements in BGPsec.

sections.title: The Problem with BGP
sections.content:
BGP is the protocol that routers use to tell each other where to send traffic on the Internet. When one network wants to announce it can reach an IP address prefix, it sends a BGP announcement with the prefix and the path of networks it traveled through (the AS path). But BGP has no built-in security: any AS can announce any prefix, and intermediate routers can modify the AS path.

RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure) provides origin validation, confirming that a network has the right to announce a prefix. But it does not sign the announcement itself, and it says nothing about whether the AS path is accurate. This document describes what requirements a more complete security protocol called BGPsec must satisfy.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP lets networks announce routes without proof of ownership. RPKI helps a little, but BGPsec needs to do more: prove the origin owns the route AND prove the path to it is real.

sections.title: Core Security Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC establishes two main goals. First, a BGPsec receiver must be able to determine with high certainty that the originating AS has the authority to announce the prefix (requirement 3.1). Second, it must determine that the AS path in the announcement accurately represents the real sequence of external BGP exchanges from the origin to the receiver, including whether any AS modified or prepended its own number (requirement 3.2).

The design must support incremental deployment, as not all networks will upgrade at once (requirement 3.4). It must operate with backward compatibility so that old and new routers can coexist (requirement 3.13). And each network must be able to choose whether to use BGPsec on a per-peer basis (requirement 3.12).
sections.plainLanguage: BGPsec must prove two things: that the sender owns the route, and that the path from origin to you is real. It must let old and new routers work together, and networks should pick which peers to secure.

sections.title: Validating BGP Update Messages
sections.content:
For BGP UPDATE messages specifically, a BGPsec design must enable recipients to formally validate that the origin AS is authorized to originate the prefix (requirement 4.1). It must go further than just checking that a path is not impossible; the design SHOULD allow the AS path to be authenticated as the message is processed (requirements 4.5 and 4.2).

The design SHOULD provide a mechanism to control replay attacks, where an attacker replays an old UPDATE message to make a router think a route is still valid when the origin has withdrawn it (requirement 4.3). Output from BGPsec validation must be unequivocal, leaving no ambiguity about whether a route is authenticated (requirement 4.7).
sections.plainLanguage: When routers get a route announcement, BGPsec must prove the origin really sent it and the path is real. It should stop old fake copies of announcements from fooling routers.

sections.title: Design Constraints and Assumptions
sections.content:
BGPsec must resist attackers with access to inter-router links, using mechanisms like TCP-AO, IPsec, or TLS to authenticate all data (requirement 3.8). The design may require new hardware and increased processing, and such costs are not forbidden (requirement 3.6). It need not prevent attacks on data-plane traffic or guarantee that data actually follows the control-plane path (requirement 3.7).

The design may use a security infrastructure like a public key infrastructure (PKI) to distribute authenticated information about address space ownership and AS numbers (requirement 3.9). However, it MUST NOT require operators to reveal more about their networks than they currently do, other than necessary security credentials (requirement 3.18). Local routing policy remains the final arbiter of which routes are used, even after BGPsec validates them (requirement 3.14).
sections.plainLanguage: BGPsec can use encryption and keys to prove authenticity. It should not slow routers too much, and networks must not have to reveal business secrets. In the end, each network picks which routes to use.

sections.title: What BGPsec Does Not Cover
sections.content:
BGPsec does not address business relationship conformance; while important to operators, these are outside the scope of security. It also does not need to secure other BGP attributes besides the AS path, which are used only locally or between immediate neighbors and may be modified in transit (requirement 3.3). AS_SET aggregation (where multiple ASes claim to originate routes together) need not be secured (requirement 3.10).

The design should support transparent route servers and AS aliasing techniques like AS migration (requirements 3.15 and 3.16). Any inter-AS use of hashes or signatures must support algorithm agility so that cryptographic algorithms can be changed as threats evolve (requirement 3.21). Security events must be logged or reported via SNMP for operators to monitor (requirement 3.19).
sections.plainLanguage: BGPsec focuses only on proving origin and path are real. It does not cover business rules, merging announcements, or the actual data transmission. It should adapt as new encryption methods become needed.
